title: Cell Biology for Medicine
summary: The cell machinery whose failures cause disease.

lessons.title: Organelles and Their Diseases

levels.kid:
Your body is made of trillions of tiny cells. Each cell is like a little city with workers inside called organelles.

The nucleus is city hall, where the instruction book (DNA) is kept. Mitochondria are power plants that make energy. Lysosomes are garbage trucks that break down trash.

If one worker team breaks, people can get sick. If the garbage trucks don't work, trash piles up inside cells. If the power plants are weak, muscles and the brain get tired, because they need lots of energy.

Doctors learn which worker is broken so they understand the sickness.
levels.hs:
Cells contain organelles, each with a job. When one fails, specific diseases follow.
- **Nucleus**: holds DNA. Mutations in genes cause inherited diseases and cancer.
- **Mitochondria**: make ATP, the cell's energy currency, through aerobic respiration. They have their own small DNA inherited only from the mother. Mitochondrial diseases hit high-energy organs hardest: brain, muscles, heart, eyes.
- **Endoplasmic reticulum (ER)**: rough ER makes proteins for export; smooth ER makes lipids and detoxifies drugs. In cystic fibrosis, the most common mutation makes the CFTR protein fold wrongly, so it gets stuck in the ER and destroyed instead of reaching the cell surface.
- **Golgi apparatus**: packages and tags proteins and ships them to the right place.
- **Lysosomes**: digest old parts and molecules using enzymes. If an enzyme is missing, its target builds up: these are lysosomal storage diseases, like Tay-Sachs (fatty molecules build up in nerve cells) and Gaucher disease.
- **Peroxisomes**: break down very long fatty acids. Failure causes disorders like X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy, which damages the brain's white matter.
- **Cilia**: hair-like projections that sweep mucus out of the airways. In primary ciliary dyskinesia they don't beat properly, causing repeated lung and sinus infections.

The big idea: knowing which organelle fails explains which organs get sick.
levels.college:
Organelle pathology maps molecular defects to clinical phenotypes.

**Endoplasmic reticulum.** Misfolded proteins are retained and degraded via ER-associated degradation (ERAD); accumulation triggers the unfolded protein response. CFTR ΔF508 (now often written F508del) misfolds and is degraded, reducing chloride transport. Alpha-1 antitrypsin Z variant polymerizes in hepatocyte ER, causing liver disease (inclusions that stain with PAS, diastase-resistant) while low circulating levels allow neutrophil elastase to destroy lung tissue (panacinar emphysema).

**Golgi and trafficking.** In I-cell disease (mucolipidosis II), defective phosphotransferase prevents addition of mannose-6-phosphate, so lysosomal enzymes are secreted instead of delivered to lysosomes; plasma enzyme levels are high while cells fill with inclusions.

**Lysosomes.** Mostly autosomal recessive enzyme deficiencies (Fabry disease and Hunter syndrome are X-linked).
- Tay-Sachs: hexosaminidase A deficiency → GM2 ganglioside accumulation; neurodegeneration, cherry-red macula, no hepatosplenomegaly.
- Gaucher: glucocerebrosidase deficiency → hepatosplenomegaly, bone crises, pancytopenia; 'crumpled tissue paper' macrophages. Enzyme replacement is available.
- Niemann-Pick type A: sphingomyelinase deficiency → neurodegeneration, hepatosplenomegaly, cherry-red spot.
- Pompe: acid maltase (acid alpha-glucosidase) deficiency → glycogen in lysosomes, cardiomyopathy in infants.

**Mitochondria.** Maternal inheritance of mtDNA; heteroplasmy (mixed normal and mutant mtDNA) and threshold effects explain variable severity. Examples: MELAS (mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis and stroke-like episodes), MERRF (myoclonic epilepsy with ragged red fibers), Leber hereditary optic neuropathy. Many mitochondrial disorders are actually caused by nuclear genes and inherited in Mendelian fashion.

**Peroxisomes.** Zellweger spectrum (biogenesis defect: hypotonia, seizures, liver dysfunction); X-ALD (ABCD1 transporter, very long chain fatty acid accumulation, adrenal insufficiency and demyelination).

**Cilia.** Primary ciliary dyskinesia (dynein arm defects): bronchiectasis, sinusitis, male infertility; with situs inversus it is called Kartagener syndrome.
levels.phd:
Organelles are not isolated compartments but a communicating network, and many diseases reflect failures of inter-organelle contact and quality control.

**Proteostasis.** The unfolded protein response has three ER sensors: IRE1 (splicing XBP1 mRNA), PERK (phosphorylating eIF2α to reduce translation and inducing ATF4 and CHOP) and ATF6 (cleaved in the Golgi to an active transcription factor). Adaptive at first, chronic UPR activation becomes pro-apoptotic and contributes to beta-cell failure, neurodegeneration and some myelinopathies. Pharmacological chaperones and correctors exploit folding: CFTR modulators combine correctors that improve folding and trafficking of F508del with a potentiator that increases channel open probability, a landmark of mechanism-based therapy.

**Autophagy-lysosome axis.** The lysosome is a signaling hub: mTORC1 is activated on its surface by amino acids, and TFEB, a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis, is released to the nucleus when mTORC1 is inactive. Defective autophagy and lysosomal function are implicated in neurodegeneration. A striking example: heterozygous GBA mutations, the gene for glucocerebrosidase, are among the strongest genetic risk factors for Parkinson disease, linking a lysosomal storage gene to alpha-synuclein aggregation.

**Mitochondrial quality control.** PINK1 accumulates on depolarized mitochondria and recruits the E3 ligase Parkin to tag them for mitophagy; loss-of-function mutations cause early-onset familial Parkinson disease. Mitochondria also integrate apoptosis (cytochrome c release) and innate immunity (mtDNA released into the cytosol activates cGAS-STING; MAVS signaling on the outer membrane).

**Membrane contact sites** between ER and mitochondria regulate calcium transfer and lipid synthesis; disruption is implicated in neurodegenerative disease.

**Primary cilia** are distinct from motile cilia: non-motile sensory antennae that concentrate Hedgehog signaling machinery. Ciliopathies such as Bardet-Biedl, Joubert syndrome (molar tooth sign on MRI) and polycystic kidney disease arise from primary cilia dysfunction, explaining their multi-organ involvement. Hedgehog pathway mutations also drive medulloblastoma subgroups, connecting organelle biology to pediatric neuro-oncology.
levels.expert:
Clinically, organelle diseases are recognized by patterns rather than by organelle names.

- **Multi-system disease involving high-energy organs** (brain, muscle, heart, retina, cochlea), with exercise intolerance, raised lactate, ptosis or ophthalmoplegia, and maternal family history, suggests mitochondrial disease. Stroke-like episodes not respecting vascular territories, especially posterior, in a young person should prompt consideration of MELAS. Genetic testing (mtDNA and nuclear gene panels or exome) has largely replaced muscle biopsy as the first test. Avoid known mitochondrial toxins when possible (for example valproate in POLG-related disease, where it can cause fulminant liver failure).
- **Developmental regression in a previously normal infant**, with organomegaly or a cherry-red spot, suggests a lysosomal storage disorder. Early diagnosis matters because enzyme replacement, substrate reduction or hematopoietic stem cell transplantation work best before irreversible neurological damage, and several disorders are now included in newborn screening programs. Enzyme replacement generally does not cross the blood-brain barrier, a major limitation for neurological forms.
- **Adrenal insufficiency in a boy, or behavioral and school decline**, warrants checking very long chain fatty acids for X-ALD. MRI shows characteristic posterior white matter changes, and early transplantation or gene therapy can halt cerebral disease, so timing is everything.
- **Recurrent sinopulmonary infections from infancy, neonatal respiratory distress, situs abnormalities**: think primary ciliary dyskinesia; nasal nitric oxide is a screening test.
- **Young adult with emphysema at the lung bases plus liver disease**: check alpha-1 antitrypsin level and phenotype.

For neurosurgery, the ciliopathies and storage disorders appear indirectly: hydrocephalus in some mucopolysaccharidoses, craniovertebral junction instability and cord compression from atlantoaxial abnormalities in Morquio syndrome, and the anesthetic airway challenges these patients bring. Knowing the underlying cell biology helps anticipate those complications.

keyPoints: Mitochondria: ATP; mtDNA is maternally inherited; disease hits brain, muscle, heart, retina
Lysosomal storage diseases: missing enzyme → substrate builds up (Tay-Sachs, Gaucher, Pompe)
ER: misfolded proteins retained and degraded (CFTR F508del, alpha-1 antitrypsin Z)
I-cell disease: no mannose-6-phosphate tag, lysosomal enzymes secreted instead of delivered
Peroxisomes break down very long chain fatty acids (X-ALD, Zellweger); cilia defects cause PCD/Kartagener

test.q: Which organelle produces most of the cell's ATP?
test.explain: Mitochondria carry out oxidative phosphorylation, generating most ATP.

test.q: Mitochondrial DNA is inherited from:
test.explain: Mitochondria in the embryo come from the egg, so mtDNA is maternally inherited.

test.q: Which organs are most affected by mitochondrial disease?
choices: Skin and sweat glands, which divide quickly
Bones and cartilage, which store the most energy
High-energy organs like brain, muscle and heart
Hair and nails, which grow continuously
test.explain: Tissues with the highest energy demand fail first when ATP production is impaired.

test.q: Lysosomal storage diseases result from:
choices: Extra chromosomes copied during cell division
Missing lysosomal enzymes causing substrate buildup
Faulty cilia that fail to clear cellular waste
Too many mitochondria building up in cells
test.explain: Without the enzyme, its substrate accumulates within lysosomes.

test.q: Tay-Sachs disease is caused by deficiency of:
test.explain: Hexosaminidase A deficiency causes GM2 ganglioside accumulation in neurons.

test.q: In cystic fibrosis with the F508del mutation, the CFTR protein:
choices: Misfolds and is retained and degraded in the ER
Is made in mitochondria instead of the ER
Is made perfectly but in excessive amounts
Is sent to lysosomes for long-term storage rather than degradation
test.explain: Misfolded CFTR is recognized by ER quality control and degraded, so little reaches the cell surface.

test.q: I-cell disease results from failure to add which tag to lysosomal enzymes?
test.explain: Without mannose-6-phosphate, enzymes are secreted rather than sent to lysosomes.

test.q: Primary ciliary dyskinesia with situs inversus is called:
test.explain: Kartagener syndrome = PCD + situs inversus, from defective ciliary dynein.

test.q: Peroxisomal defects classically cause buildup of:
test.explain: Peroxisomes perform beta-oxidation of very long chain fatty acids; X-ALD shows VLCFA accumulation.

test.q: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (Z variant) damages which two organs?
test.explain: Retained protein injures hepatocytes; low circulating levels allow elastase-mediated emphysema.

test.q: Gaucher disease is caused by deficiency of ___.
test.explain: Glucocerebrosidase deficiency causes glucocerebroside accumulation in macrophages.

test.q: Which organelle packages proteins and adds sorting tags before shipping them?
test.explain: The Golgi modifies, sorts and packages proteins.

test.q: What is the term for a mix of normal and mutant mitochondrial DNA in one cell?
test.explain: Heteroplasmy, and the threshold at which mutant mtDNA causes dysfunction, explain variable severity.

kidTest.q: Organelles are like:
kidTest.explain: Each organelle has a job inside the cell.

kidTest.q: Which organelle is the power plant?
kidTest.explain: Mitochondria make energy for the cell.

kidTest.q: Lysosomes are like:
kidTest.explain: Lysosomes break down trash inside the cell.

kidTest.q: The nucleus keeps the:
kidTest.explain: DNA, the cell's instructions, is kept in the nucleus.

kidTest.q: If garbage trucks break, what happens?
choices: Trash piles up in the cell
kidTest.explain: Without working lysosomes, waste builds up and the cell gets sick.

kidTest.q: What tiny building blocks is your body made of? (5 letters)
kidTest.explain: Your body is made of trillions of cells.

advancedTest.q: Heterozygous mutations in GBA (glucocerebrosidase) are a major genetic risk factor for which disease?
advancedTest.explain: GBA links lysosomal dysfunction to alpha-synuclein aggregation and Parkinson disease.

advancedTest.q: PINK1 and Parkin mutations cause early-onset Parkinson disease by impairing:
advancedTest.explain: PINK1 accumulates on depolarized mitochondria and recruits Parkin to tag them for autophagic clearance.

advancedTest.q: Why does enzyme replacement therapy often fail to treat the neurological features of lysosomal storage diseases?
choices: Neurological features are not caused by storage
The enzymes do not cross the blood-brain barrier
advancedTest.explain: Large recombinant enzymes cannot cross the BBB in useful amounts, so CNS disease progresses.

advancedTest.q: A child with a 'molar tooth sign' on MRI, hypotonia and abnormal breathing likely has a disorder of:
advancedTest.explain: Joubert syndrome is a ciliopathy with cerebellar vermis hypoplasia and the molar tooth sign.

lessons.title: The Cell Cycle and Its Checkpoints

levels.kid:
Cells make new cells by splitting in two. That's how you grow and how a cut heals.

But before a cell splits, it has to copy its instruction book perfectly. Then it checks its work, like you checking your homework before handing it in.

There are safety guards called checkpoints. If a guard finds a mistake, it says "Stop! Fix it first." If the mistake is too big, the guard tells the cell to retire for good.

Cancer happens when the guards stop doing their job, and cells keep splitting and splitting, even when they shouldn't.
levels.hs:
The cell cycle is the series of steps a cell goes through to divide:
- **G1 (gap 1)**: the cell grows and does its normal job. It decides whether to divide.
- **S (synthesis)**: DNA is copied, so each chromosome now has two identical sister chromatids.
- **G2 (gap 2)**: the cell checks the copied DNA and prepares to divide.
- **M (mitosis)**: chromosomes are separated into two new nuclei, then the cell splits (cytokinesis).
- **G0**: a resting state. Many cells, like most neurons, leave the cycle and rarely or never divide again.

**Checkpoints** stop the cycle if something is wrong:
- G1/S checkpoint: is the DNA damaged? Is the environment right for dividing?
- G2/M checkpoint: was DNA copied correctly?
- Spindle checkpoint (during mitosis): are all chromosomes attached properly before they are pulled apart?

The proteins that drive the cycle are **cyclins** and **cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs)**. Brakes include **p53**, called the "guardian of the genome," which halts the cycle or triggers cell death when DNA is damaged, and **Rb (retinoblastoma protein)**, which holds back the move from G1 into S.

Cancer comes from mutations that press the gas pedal (oncogenes) or break the brakes (tumor suppressor genes like p53 and Rb). Many chemotherapy drugs attack dividing cells, which is why hair follicles, gut lining and bone marrow, which also divide fast, are affected.
levels.college:
**Drivers.** Cyclin-CDK complexes phosphorylate targets to advance the cycle: cyclin D-CDK4/6 in early G1, cyclin E-CDK2 at G1/S, cyclin A-CDK2 in S, cyclin B-CDK1 at G2/M. CDK activity is restrained by CDK inhibitors: the INK4 family (p16 inhibits CDK4/6) and the Cip/Kip family (p21, p27).

**The restriction point.** Hypophosphorylated Rb binds E2F transcription factors, blocking S-phase genes. Growth-factor signaling raises cyclin D; cyclin D-CDK4/6 (then cyclin E-CDK2) phosphorylates Rb, releasing E2F and committing the cell to S phase.

**DNA damage response.** Damage activates the kinases ATM (double-strand breaks) and ATR (replication stress), which activate CHK2 and CHK1 and stabilize p53. p53 induces p21 (G1 arrest), DNA repair genes, and pro-apoptotic genes (such as BAX, PUMA and NOXA). MDM2 normally ubiquitinates p53 for degradation and is itself induced by p53, forming a feedback loop.

**Spindle assembly checkpoint.** Unattached kinetochores generate a signal (MAD2, BUBR1) that inhibits the anaphase-promoting complex/cyclosome (APC/C) bound to CDC20. When all kinetochores are attached, APC/C ubiquitinates securin (freeing separase to cleave cohesin) and cyclin B, allowing anaphase and mitotic exit. Failure causes aneuploidy.

**Cancer genetics.** Oncogenes are gain-of-function and act dominantly at the cellular level (RAS, MYC, cyclin D amplification). Tumor suppressors require loss of both alleles (Knudson two-hit hypothesis): in hereditary retinoblastoma, one RB1 mutation is inherited and a second is acquired, causing early, often bilateral tumors. Li-Fraumeni syndrome (germline TP53) causes diverse early cancers, including brain tumors. High-risk HPV E6 targets p53 for degradation and E7 inactivates Rb, explaining cervical and oropharyngeal cancer.

**Pharmacology link.** Cell-cycle-specific drugs act in particular phases: antimetabolites in S phase, vinca alkaloids and taxanes in M phase (microtubules). CDK4/6 inhibitors are used in hormone-receptor-positive breast cancer.
levels.phd:
The cell cycle is an ordered series of irreversible transitions built from interlocking feedback loops. The G1/S transition behaves as a bistable switch: E2F induces cyclin E, cyclin E-CDK2 further phosphorylates Rb, and positive feedback converts graded mitogen signals into all-or-none commitment. Single-cell imaging has refined the classic model, showing that some cells exiting mitosis already decide between proliferation and quiescence based on CDK2 activity and inherited DNA damage from the mother cell, and that p21 levels mark a bifurcation.

Mitotic entry is similarly switch-like: cyclin B-CDK1 activates its activator CDC25 and inhibits its inhibitor WEE1, producing a rapid, hysteretic transition. Mitotic exit relies on APC/C-mediated proteolysis, and the spindle assembly checkpoint's 'wait anaphase' signal from a single unattached kinetochore can delay the entire cell through catalytic MAD2 conformational conversion.

Cancer cells typically lose G1 control (Rb pathway or p53 inactivation, present in most tumors in some form) and become dependent on the G2/M checkpoint to repair DNA, creating vulnerabilities. Synthetic lethality exploits this: PARP inhibitors kill BRCA1/2-deficient cells lacking homologous recombination; WEE1 and ATR inhibitors target checkpoint dependence in p53-deficient tumors.

Chromosomal instability, persistent mis-segregation, generates aneuploidy and intratumoral heterogeneity that fuel drug resistance. Telomere crisis and whole-genome doubling are frequent events in tumor evolution. Senescence, a stable arrest enforced by p16 and p21 with a secretory phenotype (SASP), is tumor-suppressive acutely but can promote inflammation and tumorigenesis chronically.

Post-mitotic neurons illustrate the other extreme: re-entry of neurons into the cell cycle, observed in Alzheimer disease models and after ischemia, tends to cause death rather than division. In neuro-oncology, the cell cycle explains tumor biology: CDKN2A/B homozygous deletion upgrades IDH-mutant astrocytomas to grade 4 in the WHO classification, and CDK4 amplification and RB1 loss are common in glioblastoma.
levels.expert:
Clinicians meet the cell cycle through oncology, pharmacology and genetics.

- **Toxicity patterns follow proliferation.** Cytotoxic chemotherapy damages bone marrow (neutropenia with a predictable nadir), gut mucosa (mucositis, diarrhea) and hair follicles. Febrile neutropenia in a patient on chemotherapy is an emergency treated urgently with broad-spectrum antibiotics.
- **Radiation sensitivity is phase-dependent**: cells in G2/M are most sensitive, S phase most resistant. Fractionation exploits reassortment and reoxygenation, and normal tissues' better repair capacity.
- **Hereditary cancer syndromes** often present as unusual cancers at young ages: bilateral retinoblastoma in an infant, multiple primary cancers in a family (Li-Fraumeni: sarcomas, breast cancer, brain tumors, adrenocortical carcinoma). Survivors of hereditary retinoblastoma have elevated risk of later sarcomas, especially after radiation, which influences treatment choice. Genetic counseling and surveillance protocols follow.
- **Molecular pathology drives neuro-oncology.** Modern brain tumor diagnosis integrates histology with molecular markers. In diffuse gliomas, IDH status, 1p/19q codeletion and CDKN2A/B deletion determine type and grade; MGMT promoter methylation predicts response to alkylating chemotherapy (temozolomide), which methylates DNA and depends on failed repair to kill. The neurosurgeon's job includes obtaining enough well-preserved tissue for this analysis, and maximal safe resection is a prognostic factor in many gliomas.
- **Targeted drugs acting on the cycle**: CDK4/6 inhibitors (palbociclib, ribociclib, abemaciclib) in breast cancer cause neutropenia; PARP inhibitors in BRCA-associated cancers. Knowing the mechanism predicts the side effects.
- **Wound healing and fracture repair** are proliferative processes; antiproliferative drugs and radiation impair them, relevant to timing surgery around chemotherapy and radiotherapy.

The practical thread: mechanism predicts both efficacy and toxicity, and the tumor's genetics increasingly decide the treatment.

keyPoints: Cycle: G1 → S (DNA copied) → G2 → M (mitosis); G0 = resting (most neurons)
Checkpoints: G1/S, G2/M and the spindle checkpoint stop division if something is wrong
Cyclins + CDKs drive the cycle; Rb and p53 are brakes (tumor suppressors)
Oncogenes = gain of function (gas pedal); tumor suppressors need two hits (broken brakes)
HPV E6 degrades p53, E7 inactivates Rb; chemo targets fast-dividing cells

test.q: In which phase is DNA replicated?
test.explain: S (synthesis) phase is when DNA is copied.

test.q: Most mature neurons are in which state?
test.explain: Most neurons are post-mitotic and remain in G0.

test.q: Which protein is called the 'guardian of the genome'?
test.explain: p53 halts the cycle or triggers apoptosis in response to DNA damage.

test.q: Hypophosphorylated Rb prevents entry into S phase by binding:
test.explain: Rb sequesters E2F; phosphorylation by CDKs releases E2F to activate S-phase genes.

test.q: Which checkpoint ensures all chromosomes are attached to the spindle before separation?
test.explain: The spindle assembly checkpoint delays anaphase until every kinetochore is attached.

test.q: Oncogenes typically cause cancer through:
test.explain: Oncogenes are overactive versions of growth-promoting genes; one activated allele can be enough.

test.q: The Knudson two-hit hypothesis applies to:
test.explain: Both copies of a tumor suppressor must be lost; hereditary cases inherit the first hit.

test.q: High-risk HPV protein E6 promotes cancer by:
test.explain: E6 degrades p53; E7 inactivates Rb.

test.q: Why do chemotherapy drugs often cause hair loss and mouth sores?
choices: Hair follicles and mucosa divide rapidly
They trigger autoimmune attack on skin
test.explain: Many cytotoxic drugs target dividing cells, including normal rapidly dividing tissues.

test.q: p21 causes cell-cycle arrest by:
test.explain: p21 is a CDK inhibitor induced by p53.

test.q: Cyclins activate cyclin-dependent ___ (abbreviated CDKs).
test.explain: CDKs are kinases that phosphorylate cell-cycle targets when bound to cyclins.

test.q: Name the phase in which the cell divides its nucleus (one letter or the full word).
test.explain: M phase includes mitosis and cytokinesis.

test.q: Which tumor suppressor gene is mutated in hereditary retinoblastoma? (gene symbol)
test.explain: RB1 encodes the Rb protein; one germline hit plus one acquired hit causes the tumor.

kidTest.q: How do cells make new cells?
kidTest.explain: Cells divide into two to make new cells.

kidTest.q: Before splitting, a cell must copy its:
kidTest.explain: The DNA has to be copied so both new cells get a full set.

kidTest.q: Checkpoints are like:
choices: Safety guards that check for mistakes
Traffic jams that make cells wait
kidTest.explain: Checkpoints stop the cell if something went wrong.

kidTest.q: Cancer happens when:
choices: Cells take a long nap and forget to wake up
You eat too many vegetables at dinner time
The guards stop working and cells keep splitting
kidTest.explain: When checkpoints fail, cells can divide out of control.

kidTest.q: Cell splitting helps you:
kidTest.explain: New cells help you grow and repair your body.

kidTest.q: What disease happens when cells keep splitting when they shouldn't? (6 letters)
kidTest.explain: Cancer is uncontrolled cell division.

advancedTest.q: PARP inhibitors are especially effective in BRCA1/2-mutant tumors because of:
choices: Synthetic lethality with defective homologous recombination repair
Inhibition of CDK4/6, which blocks G1-S cell cycle progression
Activation of p53, which triggers apoptosis in damaged cells
Blocking microtubule assembly during mitotic spindle formation
advancedTest.explain: Cells lacking HR depend on PARP-mediated repair; blocking both is lethal to tumor but spares normal cells with one functional BRCA allele.

advancedTest.q: In the WHO CNS tumor classification, which alteration makes an IDH-mutant astrocytoma grade 4 regardless of histology?
advancedTest.explain: CDKN2A/B homozygous deletion confers grade 4 in IDH-mutant astrocytomas. 1p/19q codeletion defines oligodendroglioma.

advancedTest.q: MGMT promoter methylation in glioblastoma predicts better response to temozolomide because:
choices: Methylation tightens the blood-brain barrier around the tumor
Methylation increases tumor proliferation, raising drug uptake
MGMT activates temozolomide, so methylation boosts its effect
Silenced MGMT cannot remove the alkyl groups the drug adds to DNA
advancedTest.explain: MGMT repairs O6-alkylguanine; when silenced, temozolomide-induced lesions persist and kill tumor cells.

advancedTest.q: Why does the cyclin B-CDK1 activation at mitotic entry behave like an abrupt switch?
choices: E2F degrades cyclin B, abruptly removing an inhibitory signal
Positive feedback: CDK1 activates CDC25 and inhibits WEE1
APC/C activity is required to trigger entry into mitosis
p53 directly phosphorylates and activates cyclin B-CDK1
advancedTest.explain: Double positive feedback loops create bistability and a rapid, irreversible transition.

lessons.title: Cell Signaling

levels.kid:
Cells talk to each other using tiny chemical messages, like passing notes in class.

A message floats to a cell and fits into a special spot on its outside called a receptor, like a key fitting into a lock. When the key turns, the cell gets the message and does something, like grow, make a hormone, or squeeze.

Some messages are like a doorbell that rings a whole chain of helpers inside the cell, one after another, like dominoes falling.

If a lock gets stuck "on," the cell keeps acting even with no message. That can make people sick, so many medicines work by blocking or turning these locks.
levels.hs:
Cells communicate with chemical signals (hormones, neurotransmitters, growth factors) that bind receptors. Binding triggers a response inside the cell, often through a chain reaction called a signaling cascade.

Main receptor types:
- **G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs)**: the largest family. When activated, they switch on a G protein, which turns on enzymes that make "second messengers" like cAMP. Adrenaline acting on the heart uses this route. A large share of all medicines target GPCRs.
- **Receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs)**: receptors for growth factors and insulin. They add phosphate groups to proteins, starting cascades like the RAS pathway that tell cells to grow and divide.
- **Ion channel receptors**: open a gate for ions when a neurotransmitter binds, producing very fast responses, like nerve and muscle signals.
- **Intracellular (nuclear) receptors**: fat-soluble hormones such as cortisol, estrogen and thyroid hormone pass through the membrane and bind receptors inside the cell that directly change which genes are turned on. These responses are slower but long-lasting.

Disease examples:
- Cholera toxin locks a G protein in the "on" position, so gut cells pump out salt and water, causing massive watery diarrhea.
- Mutations that keep RAS permanently "on" are common in cancers.
- In type 2 diabetes, cells respond poorly to insulin signaling (insulin resistance).

Many drugs are agonists (turn receptors on) or antagonists (block them).
levels.college:
**GPCRs** have seven transmembrane helices and couple to heterotrimeric G proteins (α, β, γ). Ligand binding promotes GDP-to-GTP exchange on Gα; the intrinsic GTPase activity of Gα terminates signaling.
- **Gs**: activates adenylyl cyclase → ↑cAMP → protein kinase A (PKA). Examples: beta-adrenergic receptors, glucagon, vasopressin V2.
- **Gi**: inhibits adenylyl cyclase → ↓cAMP; βγ subunits open GIRK potassium channels. Examples: alpha-2 adrenergic, M2 muscarinic, opioid, D2 dopamine receptors.
- **Gq**: activates phospholipase C → PIP2 split into IP3 (releases Ca2+ from the ER) and DAG (activates protein kinase C). Examples: alpha-1 adrenergic, M1 and M3 muscarinic, H1 histamine.
Bacterial toxins exploit this: cholera toxin ADP-ribosylates Gsα and blocks its GTPase, so it stays active; pertussis toxin ADP-ribosylates Giα and prevents its activation, so inhibition of adenylyl cyclase is lost. Both raise cAMP by opposite routes.

**RTKs** (insulin receptor, EGFR, VEGFR, PDGFR) dimerize and autophosphorylate tyrosines, recruiting adaptors. Major downstream branches: RAS → RAF → MEK → ERK (proliferation) and PI3K → AKT → mTOR (growth, survival, glucose uptake). RAS is a small GTPase; oncogenic mutations impair GTP hydrolysis.

**Cytokine receptors** lack intrinsic kinase activity and use associated JAK kinases, which phosphorylate STAT transcription factors (JAK-STAT). The JAK2 V617F mutation drives polycythemia vera and other myeloproliferative neoplasms.

**Ligand-gated ion channels**: nicotinic acetylcholine, GABA-A, NMDA and AMPA glutamate receptors; millisecond responses.

**Nuclear receptors**: steroid receptors typically reside in the cytoplasm bound to heat shock proteins and translocate to the nucleus upon ligand binding; thyroid hormone receptors are already bound to DNA. They act as ligand-activated transcription factors.

**Signal termination and regulation** are as important as activation: phosphatases, phosphodiesterases (degrading cAMP and cGMP), receptor desensitization by GRKs and arrestins, and internalization. Desensitization explains tolerance to repeated agonist exposure.
levels.phd:
Signaling networks are characterized less by linear pathways than by modularity, crosstalk, feedback and spatial organization.

**Scaffolds and compartments.** A-kinase anchoring proteins (AKAPs) localize PKA with its substrates and phosphodiesterases, creating cAMP microdomains, so the same second messenger encodes different outputs in different subcellular locations. Lipid rafts, endosomes and the primary cilium act as signaling platforms; GPCRs continue signaling from endosomes after internalization.

**Biased agonism.** GPCRs adopt multiple active conformations; ligands can preferentially engage G protein or beta-arrestin pathways. This concept motivated attempts to separate therapeutic from adverse effects, for example at the mu-opioid receptor, though results have been mixed and partly attributed to differences in intrinsic efficacy rather than true bias. Allosteric modulators binding outside the orthosteric site offer subtype selectivity and 'ceiling' effects.

**Signal dynamics.** Cells decode not just amplitude but duration and frequency: transient versus sustained ERK activation in PC12 cells drives proliferation versus neuronal differentiation; NF-κB and p53 oscillate; calcium oscillation frequency regulates NFAT and other transcription factors. Negative feedback (ERK phosphorylating SOS and RAF; mTORC1-S6K inhibiting IRS-1) produces adaptation and also mediates drug resistance: blocking mTORC1 relieves feedback and can paradoxically activate AKT; BRAF inhibitors paradoxically activate ERK in BRAF-wild-type cells with active RAS via RAF dimerization, explaining secondary squamous skin tumors.

**Oncogenic signaling and targeted therapy.** Kinase-driven cancers show oncogene addiction: imatinib for BCR-ABL in chronic myeloid leukemia, EGFR inhibitors in EGFR-mutant lung cancer, BRAF and MEK inhibitors in BRAF V600E tumors, including some pediatric low-grade gliomas. Direct KRAS G12C inhibitors, exploiting a mutant cysteine next to a cryptic pocket, overturned the long-held view that RAS was undruggable. Resistance emerges through secondary target mutations, bypass pathways and lineage plasticity.

In neuroscience, receptor signaling underlies plasticity: NMDA receptor-mediated calcium influx activates CaMKII and downstream cascades that strengthen synapses (long-term potentiation), linking cell signaling to memory.
levels.expert:
Almost every drug you prescribe acts on a signaling pathway, and much of clinical reasoning is predicting effects from the receptor and its second messenger.

- **Autonomic pharmacology is GPCR pharmacology.** Alpha-1 (Gq) causes vasoconstriction; beta-1 (Gs) increases heart rate and contractility; beta-2 (Gs) relaxes bronchial and vascular smooth muscle; M2 (Gi) slows the heart; M3 (Gq) contracts the bladder and bronchi and stimulates glands. If you know the receptor, you can predict both the desired effect and the side effects of an agonist or antagonist. Selectivity is relative; it erodes as exposure rises.
- **Desensitization and tolerance.** Continuous beta-agonist exposure downregulates receptors; abrupt withdrawal of beta-blockers after chronic use can cause rebound tachycardia and ischemia because of receptor upregulation.
- **Endocrine disease is signaling disease.** Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus results from V2 receptor or aquaporin-2 defects; pseudohypoparathyroidism from Gsα mutations causing PTH resistance; activating Gsα mutations (McCune-Albright syndrome) cause endocrine hyperfunction and fibrous dysplasia. Growth hormone-secreting pituitary adenomas frequently carry activating Gsα (GNAS) mutations, relevant to the neurosurgeon who removes them through a transsphenoidal approach.
- **Steroid effects are slow and genomic.** Corticosteroids reduce peritumoral vasogenic edema around brain tumors and metastases over hours to days, through transcriptional effects; they are a mainstay of neuro-oncology but bring hyperglycemia, infection risk, myopathy and mood effects.
- **Targeted oncology**: EGFR, ALK, BRAF and other kinase inhibitors work only when the tumor carries the target alteration, so tissue and molecular testing precede therapy. Brain metastases from driver-mutated cancers sometimes respond to CNS-penetrant kinase inhibitors, changing whether surgery or radiosurgery is needed.
- **JAK inhibitors** treat myeloproliferative neoplasms and autoimmune disease but increase infection risk, a direct prediction from blocking cytokine signaling.

Mechanism-first thinking lets you handle a drug you have never prescribed: find its receptor and pathway, and you can anticipate most of what it will do.

keyPoints: GPCRs: Gs ↑cAMP, Gi ↓cAMP, Gq → PLC → IP3 (Ca2+) + DAG (PKC)
RTKs (insulin, EGFR) → RAS-MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR; RAS mutations keep growth 'on'
Cytokines use JAK-STAT; JAK2 V617F drives polycythemia vera
Steroid and thyroid hormones act on intracellular receptors that change gene transcription
Cholera toxin keeps Gs on; pertussis toxin disables Gi; both raise cAMP

test.q: The largest family of cell-surface receptors and a major drug target is:
test.explain: GPCRs are the largest receptor family and are targeted by a large share of approved drugs.

test.q: Activation of a Gs-coupled receptor causes:
test.explain: Gs stimulates adenylyl cyclase, raising cAMP and activating PKA.

test.q: Gq-coupled receptors activate:
test.explain: PLC splits PIP2 into IP3 (calcium release) and DAG (PKC activation).

test.q: Insulin acts through which receptor type?
test.explain: The insulin receptor is a tyrosine kinase that autophosphorylates and activates PI3K-AKT and MAPK pathways.

test.q: Cortisol and other steroid hormones mostly act by:
choices: Binding intracellular receptors that alter gene transcription
Activating Gq-coupled receptors that release calcium from stores
Opening sodium channels to depolarize the target cell membrane
Binding cell-surface receptor tyrosine kinases on target tissues
test.explain: Lipid-soluble steroids cross the membrane and act on nuclear receptors, a slower genomic effect.

test.q: Cholera toxin causes watery diarrhea by:
choices: Destroying intestinal cells so fluid leaks out freely
Locking Gs alpha in the active state, raising cAMP
Blocking Gs alpha so cAMP falls and chloride is retained
Inhibiting protein kinase C in the intestinal crypt cells
test.explain: ADP-ribosylation of Gsα prevents GTP hydrolysis; high cAMP drives chloride and water secretion via CFTR.

test.q: Oncogenic RAS mutations usually:
choices: Impair GTP hydrolysis so RAS stays on
test.explain: RAS is a GTPase; mutations reduce GTP hydrolysis, so it remains in the active GTP-bound state.

test.q: Cytokine receptors without their own kinase activity signal through:
test.explain: Associated Janus kinases phosphorylate STAT transcription factors.

test.q: Which receptor type produces the fastest responses (milliseconds)?
test.explain: Ion channels open directly on binding, which underlies fast synaptic transmission.

test.q: A drug that binds a receptor and blocks the natural signal is called:
test.explain: Antagonists bind without activating, preventing agonist action.

test.q: Gq signaling generates IP3, which releases ___ from the endoplasmic reticulum.
test.explain: IP3 opens ER calcium channels; DAG activates protein kinase C.

test.q: What second messenger does adenylyl cyclase make? (abbreviation)
test.explain: Adenylyl cyclase converts ATP to cyclic AMP.

test.q: Which JAK2 mutation drives polycythemia vera? (letter-number-letter)
test.explain: The JAK2 V617F mutation constitutively activates JAK-STAT signaling.

kidTest.q: How do cells talk to each other?
kidTest.explain: Cells send chemical messages to each other.

kidTest.q: A receptor is like a:
choices: Lock that a message key fits into
Hat that sits on your head
kidTest.explain: Messages fit receptors like keys fit locks.

kidTest.q: A chain of helpers inside the cell is like:
choices: A big closed door that stays shut
A sleepy cat curled up on a rug
kidTest.explain: Signals pass from helper to helper like falling dominoes.

kidTest.q: If a lock gets stuck 'on,' the cell:
choices: Keeps acting even with no message
Turns bright red and sleeps for a while
kidTest.explain: A stuck-on signal makes the cell keep working when it shouldn't.

kidTest.q: Many medicines work by:
kidTest.explain: Many drugs turn receptors on or block them.

kidTest.q: What is the 'lock' on a cell called? (starts with 'r')
kidTest.explain: A receptor receives the chemical message.

advancedTest.q: Pertussis toxin raises cAMP by a different route than cholera toxin. How?
choices: It activates Gs alpha directly by locking its GTPase activity off
It blocks protein kinase A, so cAMP accumulates without being used
It ADP-ribosylates Gi alpha, preventing inhibition of adenylyl cyclase
It inhibits phosphodiesterase, so cAMP is broken down much more slowly
advancedTest.explain: Inactivating Gi removes the brake on adenylyl cyclase; cholera toxin instead jams the accelerator (Gs).

advancedTest.q: BRAF inhibitors can cause new squamous skin lesions in patients with BRAF-mutant melanoma because they:
choices: Paradoxically activate ERK in BRAF-wild-type cells with active RAS through RAF dimerization
Are direct carcinogens to melanocytes, causing new UV-type mutations in the skin
Block JAK-STAT signaling, removing immune surveillance of keratinocytes
Inhibit p53 in keratinocytes, so damaged skin cells escape apoptosis
advancedTest.explain: In wild-type cells with upstream RAS activity, inhibitor binding promotes RAF dimers that transactivate and increase MAPK signaling.

advancedTest.q: Inhibiting mTORC1 can paradoxically increase AKT activity because:
choices: It relieves S6K-mediated negative feedback on IRS-1
mTORC1 directly inhibits AKT kinase domain
advancedTest.explain: S6K normally suppresses IRS-1; blocking mTORC1 removes this brake, enhancing PI3K-AKT signaling.

advancedTest.q: Growth hormone-secreting pituitary adenomas frequently carry activating mutations in which gene encoding Gs alpha?
advancedTest.explain: Activating GNAS mutations (gsp oncogene) raise cAMP in somatotrophs, driving GH secretion and growth.

lessons.title: Cell Death: Apoptosis and Necrosis

levels.kid:
Cells don't live forever. There are two main ways a cell can die.

The first way is neat and tidy. The cell knows it's time, packs itself into little bundles, and helper cells clean it up quietly. It's like folding up your tent at the end of a camping trip. This is called apoptosis. Your body does it all the time, and it's healthy!

The second way is messy. The cell gets hurt badly, maybe from no blood or a big injury, and bursts open. Its insides spill out and the area gets red and swollen. This is called necrosis.

Doctors see messy necrosis in heart attacks and strokes.
levels.hs:
Cells die in two main ways, and the difference matters.

**Apoptosis** is programmed, controlled cell death. The cell shrinks, its DNA is chopped into pieces, the nucleus condenses, and the cell breaks into neat packages called apoptotic bodies. Immune cells (macrophages) eat them without causing inflammation. Apoptosis is normal and essential:
- It sculpts the body during development, removing the webbing between fingers in the embryo.
- It removes damaged cells, including cells with DNA damage that could become cancer.
- It eliminates immune cells that would attack the body's own tissues.
Enzymes called **caspases** carry out apoptosis. Too little apoptosis contributes to cancer; too much contributes to neurodegenerative diseases.

**Necrosis** is uncontrolled cell death from severe injury: lack of blood flow (ischemia), toxins, infection, burns or trauma. The cell swells, its membrane bursts, and its contents leak out, triggering inflammation. Necrosis always means disease.

Types of necrosis look different under the microscope:
- **Coagulative**: cell outlines remain as "ghosts"; typical of heart attack and kidney infarcts.
- **Liquefactive**: tissue turns to liquid; typical of brain infarcts and abscesses.
- **Caseous**: cheese-like; typical of tuberculosis.
- **Fat necrosis**: seen in pancreatitis.

Doctors detect necrosis with blood tests for leaked proteins, like troponin from heart muscle.
levels.college:
**Apoptosis** pathways converge on executioner caspases (caspase-3 and -7), which cleave hundreds of substrates.
- **Intrinsic (mitochondrial) pathway**: triggered by DNA damage, growth factor withdrawal or cellular stress. BH3-only proteins (BIM, BID, PUMA, NOXA) activate BAX and BAK, which permeabilize the outer mitochondrial membrane (MOMP). Cytochrome c is released, binds APAF-1 to form the apoptosome, and activates caspase-9. Anti-apoptotic BCL-2, BCL-XL and MCL-1 restrain BAX/BAK. p53 promotes this pathway transcriptionally.
- **Extrinsic (death receptor) pathway**: Fas ligand or TNF binds death receptors, recruiting FADD and activating caspase-8. Cytotoxic T cells use Fas ligand and also perforin and granzyme B. Caspase-8 cleaves BID to tBID, linking to the intrinsic pathway.

Morphology: cell shrinkage, chromatin condensation (pyknosis), nuclear fragmentation (karyorrhexis), membrane blebbing, apoptotic bodies, intact membrane and no inflammation. Phosphatidylserine flips to the outer leaflet as an 'eat me' signal (detected with annexin V). DNA laddering on gel electrophoresis reflects internucleosomal cleavage.

**Necrosis**: cell swelling, loss of membrane integrity, karyolysis, enzyme leakage and inflammation.
- **Coagulative**: protein denaturation preserves architecture; ischemic infarcts of most solid organs (heart, kidney, spleen), but not the brain.
- **Liquefactive**: enzymatic digestion dominates; brain infarcts (high lipid, little connective tissue), abscesses.
- **Caseous**: granulomatous inflammation; tuberculosis and some fungi.
- **Fat**: lipase release in pancreatitis; fatty acids bind calcium (saponification).
- **Fibrinoid**: immune complex deposition in vessel walls; vasculitis, malignant hypertension.
- **Gangrenous**: ischemic limb, dry (coagulative) or wet (superimposed infection).

**Clinical relevance**: BCL-2 overexpression from the t(14;18) translocation drives follicular lymphoma by blocking apoptosis; the BCL-2 inhibitor venetoclax treats chronic lymphocytic leukemia. Defective Fas signaling causes autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome.
levels.phd:
The apoptosis-necrosis dichotomy has given way to a spectrum of regulated cell death (RCD) programs, defined by molecular mechanism as formalized by the Nomenclature Committee on Cell Death.

- **Necroptosis**: when caspase-8 is inhibited, RIPK1 and RIPK3 form the necrosome and phosphorylate MLKL, which oligomerizes and ruptures the plasma membrane. It is lytic and inflammatory, a host defense against viruses that block caspases, and contributes to ischemia-reperfusion injury and neurodegeneration.
- **Pyroptosis**: inflammasome activation (for example NLRP3) activates caspase-1 (or caspase-4/5/11 in non-canonical pathways), which cleaves gasdermin D; its N-terminal fragment forms membrane pores, releasing IL-1β and IL-18. Central to sepsis and sterile inflammation.
- **Ferroptosis**: iron-dependent lipid peroxidation when glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) or cystine import fails. Implicated in neuronal death after intracerebral hemorrhage, where iron from hemoglobin breakdown is abundant, and a target in therapy-resistant cancers.
- **Parthanatos**: excessive PARP-1 activation after DNA damage, NAD+ depletion and AIF translocation, relevant to excitotoxic neuronal death.
- **NETosis**: neutrophil extracellular trap release.

Cell death in the ischemic brain is heterogeneous. The infarct core dies rapidly by necrosis from energy failure, while the penumbra, electrically silent but viable tissue, undergoes delayed death through excitotoxicity (glutamate-driven NMDA calcium overload), oxidative stress, inflammation and regulated death programs. Reperfusion adds injury via reactive oxygen species and inflammatory cell influx. Decades of neuroprotective agents targeting these pathways succeeded in animals but failed in human trials, attributed to heterogeneous patients, narrow time windows and poor translational models; reperfusion itself remains the only proven way to rescue penumbra.

Damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) released by lytic death, including HMGB1, ATP and mtDNA, activate pattern recognition receptors and link death mode to immunity. Immunogenic cell death, induced by certain chemotherapies and radiation, can prime antitumor T-cell responses, a rationale for combining these with immunotherapy.
levels.expert:
Clinically, cell death is visible as biomarkers, imaging and histology, and the type of death predicts what happens next.

- **Biomarkers of necrosis**: troponin (myocardium), CK (skeletal muscle; massive in rhabdomyolysis, which threatens the kidneys via myoglobin and hyperkalemia), transaminases (hepatocytes), lipase (pancreas), LDH (many tissues; also a marker of tumor lysis and hemolysis). Rising and falling patterns help time the injury.
- **Tumor lysis syndrome**: rapid death of a large, chemosensitive tumor burden releases potassium, phosphate and uric acid, causing arrhythmia, kidney injury and seizures. Risk assessment and preventive measures before therapy matter.
- **Brain infarction evolves.** Ischemic neurons show 'red neurons' at 12 to 24 hours; liquefactive necrosis and macrophage infiltration follow over days, and a fluid-filled cystic cavity remains after weeks to months. Cytotoxic edema appears early on diffusion-weighted MRI (restricted diffusion), within minutes, long before CT changes. Large hemispheric infarcts swell maximally around days 2 to 5, which is when malignant edema can cause herniation and decompressive craniectomy may be considered.
- **Perfusion imaging and the penumbra.** CT or MR perfusion estimates core versus salvageable tissue, selecting patients for thrombectomy well beyond the earlier time windows. Treatment aims to rescue cells that have not yet committed to death.
- **Radiation necrosis versus tumor progression.** After radiosurgery or radiotherapy for brain tumors, enhancing lesions may be necrosis rather than recurrence. Perfusion MRI, spectroscopy, PET and sometimes biopsy help distinguish them, a common neurosurgical dilemma since management differs completely.
- **Glioblastoma histology** includes pseudopalisading necrosis, a hallmark feature of high-grade tumors.

Therapeutically, many cancer treatments work by inducing apoptosis (DNA-damaging agents acting through p53, BCL-2 inhibition with venetoclax), and resistance often reflects broken apoptotic machinery. Understanding which death program is active points to where treatment can intervene.

keyPoints: Apoptosis: programmed, caspase-driven, cell shrinks, no inflammation; normal in development
Intrinsic pathway: BAX/BAK, cytochrome c, apoptosome, caspase-9; extrinsic: Fas/TNF, caspase-8
Necrosis: swelling, membrane rupture, inflammation; always pathological
Coagulative (heart, kidney), liquefactive (brain, abscess), caseous (TB), fat (pancreatitis)
BCL-2 blocks apoptosis: t(14;18) follicular lymphoma; venetoclax inhibits BCL-2

test.q: Programmed cell death without inflammation is called:
test.explain: Apoptosis is controlled and non-inflammatory; necrosis causes inflammation.

test.q: Which enzymes carry out apoptosis?
test.explain: Caspases are proteases that dismantle the cell in an orderly way.

test.q: The removal of webbing between fingers in the embryo is an example of:
test.explain: Developmental sculpting relies on programmed cell death.

test.q: What type of necrosis occurs in a brain infarct?
test.explain: The brain's high lipid and enzyme content and scant connective tissue produce liquefaction.

test.q: A heart attack produces which type of necrosis?
test.explain: Ischemic infarcts of the heart and kidney show coagulative necrosis with preserved cell outlines.

test.q: Cheese-like (caseous) necrosis is classic for:
test.explain: Caseous necrosis occurs in granulomas of TB and some fungal infections.

test.q: In the intrinsic pathway, which molecule released from mitochondria forms the apoptosome?
test.explain: Cytochrome c binds APAF-1 to form the apoptosome, activating caspase-9.

test.q: Fas ligand and TNF trigger which apoptosis pathway?
test.explain: Death receptors recruit FADD and activate caspase-8.

test.q: Overexpression of BCL-2 promotes cancer by:
test.explain: BCL-2 prevents BAX/BAK activation, so damaged cells survive, as in follicular lymphoma with t(14;18).

test.q: Fat necrosis with saponification is typical of:
test.explain: Released lipases digest fat; fatty acids bind calcium, forming chalky deposits.

test.q: In apoptosis, ___ flips to the outer membrane as an 'eat me' signal for macrophages.
test.explain: Exposed phosphatidylserine marks apoptotic cells for quiet removal (detected with annexin V).

test.q: Which blood test protein is released by necrotic heart muscle?
test.explain: Troponin leaks from dying cardiomyocytes and is the key biomarker of MI.

test.q: Name the BCL-2 inhibitor used in chronic lymphocytic leukemia.
test.explain: Venetoclax restores apoptosis in BCL-2-dependent cancer cells.

kidTest.q: Which kind of cell death is neat and tidy?
kidTest.explain: Apoptosis is the neat, planned way cells die.

kidTest.q: Apoptosis is like:
choices: A loud thunderstorm that lasts through the night
Folding up your tent after camping
A big balloon that pops with a bang
kidTest.explain: The cell packs itself up neatly so it can be cleaned away.

kidTest.q: Necrosis happens when a cell:
kidTest.explain: Necrosis is messy death from injury, like no blood supply.

kidTest.q: Is apoptosis healthy for your body?
choices: Only on weekends and on holidays
No, never, it always means sickness
Yes, the body does it all the time
kidTest.explain: Apoptosis removes old or damaged cells and keeps you healthy.

kidTest.q: Messy necrosis makes the area:
kidTest.explain: Spilled insides cause inflammation: redness and swelling.

kidTest.q: What is the neat, planned kind of cell death called? (starts with 'a')
kidTest.explain: Apoptosis is programmed cell death.

advancedTest.q: When caspase-8 is inhibited, TNF signaling can trigger a lytic death via RIPK1, RIPK3 and MLKL. This is:
advancedTest.explain: MLKL phosphorylated by RIPK3 oligomerizes and ruptures the membrane: necroptosis.

advancedTest.q: Iron-dependent lipid peroxidation from GPX4 failure, implicated in neuronal death after intracerebral hemorrhage, is:
advancedTest.explain: Ferroptosis depends on iron and lipid peroxides; heme breakdown in ICH supplies iron.

advancedTest.q: On imaging after stroke, the ischemic penumbra is:
choices: Tissue that has liquefied, yet can still recover after reperfusion
Normal, well-perfused tissue far from the core of the stroke
Hypoperfused, dysfunctional but still viable tissue that reperfusion can rescue
Hemorrhage surrounding the infarct core after reperfusion
advancedTest.explain: Perfusion imaging distinguishes the core from salvageable penumbra, guiding thrombectomy.

advancedTest.q: Pyroptosis is executed by pores formed from:
choices: Gasdermin D cleaved by inflammatory caspases
BAX and BAK oligomers in the outer membrane
advancedTest.explain: Caspase-1 (or 4/5/11) cleaves gasdermin D; its N-terminal domain forms pores and releases IL-1β and IL-18.
